steps: Find every hexagon first: each sequence must start (or end) at one.
From each hexagon, check all 8 directions for circle, square, triangle in that order.
Also check from each triangle backwards; it is the same sequence read the other way, so do not count it twice.
The sequence appears 4 times.
qs.trap: Counting a sequence twice by reading it forwards from one end and backwards from the other.

steps: Each straight grid side is 7 units.
Each quarter circle of radius 7 is 2 × 22/7 × 7 ÷ 4 = 11 units.
For each path, count its straight sides and quarter arcs, then add 7 × sides + 11 × arcs.
The longest path comes to about 133 units.
qs.trap: Measuring an arc as if it were straight (7). A quarter circle of radius 7 is 11 long.

steps: The shown star fills the wide end. More stars must fit the narrowing tail.
Each new star has to touch both slanted sides (and the end) at 4 points, so it gets smaller as the boundary narrows.
Place stars one after another towards the tip until the next one cannot touch 4 points.
Six stars fit, including the one shown.
qs.trap: Forgetting the 4-point rule. Tiny stars that touch only two points do not count.

steps: Aim for the longest ladders: 11 › 47 and 49 › 92.
Throw 5 then 6 reaches 11 and climbs to 47. A 2 reaches 49 and climbs to 92.
The 4th throw must be 3: 92 › 95. Then a 5 lands exactly on 100.
Total: 5 throws. We checked every shorter route by computer search; none works.

steps: Split the picture into zones: upper balcony, background crowd, middle aisle, front figures.
Count heads in each zone; a figure counts even if only a head or shoulder shows.
Watch for small figures in the balcony and behind counters.
The total is 27.
qs.trap: Missing small background heads or counting a reflection or poster as a person.

steps: From the figure, each hexagon's side is half of the one before it.
Area grows with the square of the side: halving the side divides the area by 4. So 720, 180, 45.
The smallest hexagon is a cube drawing made of 3 equal rhombi.
The shaded part is 2 of the 3 rhombi: 2/3 × 45 = 30.

steps: Start with the sphere's own curved surface.
A tetrahedron passing through leaves a tunnel with flat walls, one for each face it cuts.
The cone leaves a tunnel with a curved conical wall.
Add all the separate surfaces: the official total is 6.
qs.trap: Counting the two tunnel openings as surfaces. Openings are holes, not faces.

steps: Call the first leg D at speed v. The second leg is 0.3D at 2v.
Time = D/v + 0.3D/2v = 1.15 D/v.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 1.3D ÷ 1.15D/v = 1.13v = 26, so v = 23.
Second-leg speed = 2 × 23 = 46 km/h.

steps: Compare the pictures in a grid: top-left, top-right, middle, bottom.
Check colours, objects on the floor, expressions, hair ribbons, items on the shelf.
Tick each difference on both pictures so you do not count it twice.
There are 9 differences.
qs.trap: Scanning randomly. A fixed order finds small changes faster.

steps: Look for cat heads: two pointed ears are the easiest clue.
Follow each body to a tail so you do not count a shape twice.
Darker pink shows where two cats overlap.
There are 11 cats.
qs.trap: Counting tails and ears separately. Match each pair of ears to one tail.

steps: Opposite: relative speed 110 km/h (30.6 m/s). In 9 s they cover both lengths: 275 m.
Same way: relative speed 10 km/h (2.78 m/s). The person passes the slow train's length in 18 s: 50 m.
So the fast train is 275 − 50 = 225 m long.
Seen from the slow train: 225 ÷ 2.78 = 81 s.

qs.trap: Using both train lengths for the "person" cases. A person is a point: only one train's length counts.

steps: The profile from P rises in a straight line to radius 1 at x = 4: turning it gives a cone (r 1, h 4).
From x = 4 to 6 the profile is a quarter circle of radius 2: turning it gives a half sphere.
Cone = 1/3 × pi × 1 × 4 = 4pi/3. Half sphere = 2/3 × pi × 8 = 16pi/3.
Total = 20pi/3, about 20.95.

qs.trap: Using the black blade as the solid. The wood is the part between the blade and the axis.

steps: Jar volume = pi × 6² × 6.6, about 746.7 cm³.
A six-pointed star is made of 12 equilateral triangles of side X: area = 12 × 0.433 X².
Mould volume = 12 × 0.433 X² × 4 = 20.8 X².
X² = 746.7 ÷ 20.8 = 35.9, so X is about 6.0 cm.

steps: Each box shows several sticks, some with red (unburnt) heads in different positions.
Look for the rule linking the red heads and their positions to the number.
Test the rule on every labelled box.
Applied to the last box, it gives 20.
qs.trap: Counting red heads only. Their positions also matter.

Ways to make 4: 3+1+0 (6 orders), 2+2+0 (3), 2+1+1 (3). 4+0+0 is impossible.
Total: 12 ways.
Probability = 12 ÷ 64 = 0.1875.

steps: Characters differ by small strokes: loops, hooks and marks above or below.
Take one character, find all its copies, and cross them off.
Repeat until every character is crossed off, counting the types.
There are 23 distinct types.
qs.trap: Treating two characters as the same when one has an extra hook.

steps: An open container shows its inside: a white or light inner face at the top.
Closed boxes show only outer faces, all in shades of grey.
Scan row by row and tick each open one.
There are 21 open containers.
qs.trap: Counting tapered shapes as open by their shape. Look for the visible inside face.

steps: Seen from above, the base is an equilateral triangle; each flip moves it to a neighbouring triangle.
Triangle height = 30 × 0.866 = 26. To move forward one row needs 2 flips (one to turn over, one to cross the row).
135 ÷ 26 = 5.2, so the pyramid must cross into the 6th row: 5 rows to cross.
5 rows × 2 flips = 10 flips.

steps: Note each block's shape and size: the cube and the slanted faces are easy to spot.
For each option, find where each block sits and check that all four are used.
Check that no extra block would be needed.
A, B and C use exactly the four blocks; D does not.
qs.trap: Accepting a shape that uses three blocks plus a different piece.

steps: Magenta plus yellow makes red: lots of both gives crimson (A true).
Pink needs a little magenta and almost no yellow. 70% yellow with 15% magenta gives a pale yellow-orange (B false).
Brown needs more magenta than cyan. Equal cyan and magenta with full yellow gives an olive green (C false).
Cyan plus magenta without yellow gives purple or indigo (D true).

steps: A frame made only of triangles is rigid; a loop of four or more links can move.
Look for closed triangles and braces that lock a shape.
If every loop is a triangle or is braced, nothing moves.
A, B and D contain loops that can move; C is locked.
qs.trap: Thinking more hinges always means more movement. Triangles lock no matter how many hinges.

steps: Identify species by features: tail length and curl, face fringe, body shape.
Match each silhouette in the options to a monkey on the sheet.
Check that each group in an option belongs to one species.
A and C group the same species; B and D mix species.
qs.trap: Matching by pose only. Tails and heads tell species apart.

steps: To wave, the rod's end at the gear must move back and forth as the gear turns.
That needs the rod attached off-centre: a crank pin or slot away from the axle.
A rod fixed at the centre only spins and does not push or pull.
A, B and C give an off-centre drive; D does not.
qs.trap: Choosing designs that look neat but attach the rod at the centre.

steps: The photo looks down an aisle between two rows of pillars, with a big pillar cut off on each side.
From the plan, find spots where the camera faces along an aisle at that distance.
Rows on both sides must match the number and spacing visible.
A and D give this view; B and C do not.
qs.trap: Ignoring the plan's asymmetry. Count pillars on each side of the aisle.

steps: Read each letter one at a time, ignoring style.
Check for letters that read as something else: an n that looks like a u, or a backwards s.
An option fails if any letter reads wrongly.
B, C and D read correctly; A does not.
qs.trap: Reading the whole word at a glance. Our brain fills in wrong letters.

steps: A family keeps the same letter design; only thickness or width changes.
Compare the head-line, the shape of vowel signs and the stroke endings.
A different design (different curves and terminals) is a different family.
A, B and D are the same family; C is not.
qs.trap: Picking only words of the same weight. A family includes very light and very bold versions.

steps: Four copies around the centre must fill the square exactly.
Each piece needs a right-angle corner for the square's corner and edges that meet their neighbours.
Curved edges can work if a curve on one piece fits the matching curve on the next.
A, B and D tile the square; C does not.
qs.trap: Forgetting that flipping is allowed; some pieces work only when flipped.

steps: A coconut has three "eyes" at one end only, and husk fibres at the top end only.
So only one piece can carry the eyes or the fibres.
Check each pair: one piece with the feature, the other plain.
A and C are correct; B and D put features on both halves.
qs.trap: Forgetting that the three eyes are all on one end.

steps: At each crossing, see which ring goes over and which under. A link needs one over and one under crossing.
Trace each ring and list the rings it links with.
If every ring is joined, the rings form one chain.
A (one chain) and D (two rings have one link) are true.
qs.trap: Counting an overlap as a link. A ring lying over another at both crossings is not linked.

steps: When fitted, the bottle hangs tilted, so liquid collects at its lowest corner.
The wick must reach that lowest point to soak up the last drops.
Check each design at the fitted angle: is the wick at the lowest point?
B, C and D reach the last liquid; A does not.
qs.trap: Checking the bottle upright. Picture it tilted as it sits in the socket.

steps: A ramp's steepness depends on height and length together: steepness = height ÷ length.
B is true: both decide whether a user can manage alone.
C is false: a short ramp with a small height can be gentle enough.
D is false: a short ramp to a high entrance is steep and needs help. (A is taken as true.)
qs.trap: Forgetting the question asks for FALSE statements.

steps: Pressing the pedal pushes a rod; the rod must push the lid's lever on the correct side of its hinge.
Follow each link from the pedal to the lid, checking which way each pivot turns.
If the rod pushes on the wrong side of the hinge, the lid pulls shut.
B and C open the lid.
qs.trap: Ignoring where the rod meets the lid relative to the hinge.

From 23 September to 2 October = 10 days, starting with A: A B D C A B D C A B.
That adds A 3, B 3, D 2, C 2.
Totals: A 15, B 15, C 14, D 14. A and B are worn most.

steps: Each plane cuts each face it passes through along a straight line.
Trace where the planes cross each face, then imagine the pieces opened flat.
Check the triangle shapes and which edges stay joined.
B and C match the cut pieces.
qs.trap: Unfolding before cutting. Cut first, then open each piece.

steps: A bowl rocks unless the support base stops it in every direction.
A flat plate stops rocking only along its own length.
A cross-shaped or wide base resists rocking both ways.
C and D are steady in all directions; A and B are not.
qs.trap: Checking only one direction of push.

steps: You can see the front of the train only if the track ahead curves towards your window's side.
P is on the left side of the coach; heading north, left is west.
So the track ahead of coach 19 must bend to the west.
Option C curves that way.
qs.trap: Choosing any curve. It must bend towards your side of the train.

steps: A mould is the negative of the cake and, seen from above, is a mirror image of it.
Note positions in the cake: where the cones, house and arch sit relative to each other.
Mirror that layout and look for the mould that matches.
B matches.
qs.trap: Picking the mould with the same layout as the cake. Turning a cake out mirrors it.

steps: Each visible edge of the folded paper is either an original edge or a crease.
Count the creases meeting at the top-right corner.
Match the angles of the triangular flaps.
Option A has the right creases and angles.
qs.trap: Matching only the number of lines, not their angles.

steps: Apply moves one at a time, tracking the front face.
T+ and D+ shift the top and bottom rows of the front face sideways.
R− and L− shift the right and left columns of the front face up or down.
The result matches option C.
qs.trap: Turning a face the wrong way. "Clockwise" is as seen looking directly at that face.

steps: Pick a corner where three striped faces meet, and note the stripe directions.
In each net, find those faces and fold them around that corner in your mind.
Stripes must meet the edges in the same way as on the cube.
Only net C matches.
qs.trap: Checking faces one at a time instead of the way they meet at a corner.

steps: Track one colour at a time: black, then grey.
Find how each block moves from one grid to the next.
Apply the same change once more.
Option D follows the rule.
qs.trap: Tracking all colours at once.

steps: Only the raised (white) parts touch the ground and print.
A footprint is the mirror image of the sole as you look at it.
Check the number 3: on the print it appears reversed.
Option B shows the mirrored print.
qs.trap: Forgetting the mirroring, as with a stamp.

steps: Each property of the shape row (colour, shape, fill, count) changes one face.
Compare rows that differ in only one property to find which face it controls.
Build the row for two filled blue triangles.
Option A fits.
qs.trap: Trying to read all four faces at once. Isolate one property at a time.

steps: Spinning the curve around Y makes a rounded rod along Y.
Two clones at 120° around X add two rods splayed down, like a tripod.
A copy turned 90° around Y adds two more splayed rods; the upright rod stays put.
Result: one upright rod with four legs, option B.

steps: A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
So the Earth must be between the Sun and the Moon: Sun, Earth, Moon.
Moon between Sun and Earth is a solar eclipse.
Option B shows Sun, Earth, Moon.

qs.trap: Mixing up lunar and solar eclipses. Lunar = Moon in Earth's shadow.

steps: A paddle pushing water backwards pushes the boat forwards on that side.
To turn right, the left side must be pushed forward more, or the right side held back.
Check each option's paddles and push directions.
Option D turns the boat right.
qs.trap: Thinking the boat turns towards the side that paddles harder. It turns away from it.

steps: At 45°, a shadow is as long as the height of whatever casts it.
Use the top view and side view to find the height of each block.
Each shadow falls to the right of its block by that height.
Option D shows the correct shadows.
qs.trap: Drawing shadows without using the block heights.

steps: Count the faces of the solid: squares and triangles.
Check that each net has the right number of each.
Fold the net in your mind, checking where the triangles meet.
Only D folds correctly.
qs.trap: Accepting a net with the right faces in the wrong places.

steps: A cover must slide in, lock and come out again.
It needs guide rails that match grooves in the body, and a latch that clicks into a slot.
Check each option for matching rails and a latch with a matching slot.
Only C has both.
qs.trap: Picking a design with rails but no latch, or a latch with no slot.

steps: The most common English letters are e, t, a, o, i, n, s, r, h.
Short travel means putting these letters near the centre and the space key.
Check where each layout puts these letters.
Layout B places most of them right around the space key.

qs.trap: Choosing the layout that looks like a normal keyboard. QWERTY was not designed for short travel.

steps: The example shows a 180° rotation of the whole grid: top-left goes to bottom-right, and each symbol turns upside down.
Apply the same rotation to every symbol.
Check two or three distinctive symbols in each option.
Option B matches.
qs.trap: Moving symbols without turning each one upside down.

steps: An inside face, seen from inside, appears mirrored compared with the outside view.
Match each section to the N, E, W or S side by its pattern of openings.
Then decide whether it is seen from inside or outside.
Option B lists the correct order.
qs.trap: Forgetting that inside views are mirror images.

steps: Count the frames and joint types shown in the kit.
Follow the steps: frames lock at right angles using the pins.
Check each option for the right number of frames and possible joints.
Option B can be built.
qs.trap: Accepting a design that needs more frames than the kit has.

steps: Dye soaks the exposed outer edges of the folded roll, giving bands.
The first dye, folded along Y, gives bands in one direction.
The second, folded along X, gives bands at right angles.
Two sets of crossing bands make a grid: option C.
qs.trap: Choosing a single cross. Folding several times gives several bands.

qs.note: The animation morphs between a dog, a swan and a seal. On paper only one frame is visible, so this question is best practised with the GIF itself.

steps: Choose two clear features in the red square: a coloured block and a black bar.
Note their positions relative to each other and to the lines.
Check each option for both features in the same places.
Only D matches exactly.
qs.trap: Accepting a near match with one block a different colour.

steps: Each loud beat in a loop becomes a line in its layout; spacing follows the rhythm.
Compare the gaps between loud beats with the gaps between lines.
Match the most distinctive loop first, then the others.
P-3, Q-4, R-1, S-2: option C.
qs.trap: Counting lines only. The spacing pattern is what matches.

steps: Rolling repeats the design along the paper.
The print is the mirror image of the design as seen through the roller.
Because the roller is transparent, you see the back of the design.
D shows the correct repeated, mirrored print.
qs.trap: Forgetting to mirror the print.

steps: Look at how the stripes meet the central line in each square.
Check whether the stripes on both sides are mirror images of each other.
Three squares share one rule; one breaks it.
D is the odd one.
qs.trap: Looking at stripe thickness instead of direction.

steps: Each letter becomes one bar; the same letter always has the same height.
Count the bars: the name must have the same number of letters.
Check repeated letters: repeated heights must fall in the same places.
RADHAKRISHNAN fits the pattern.
qs.trap: Matching only the length. Several names have 13 letters; the repeats decide.

steps: Looking along the spring's axis, you see each coil as a circle.
The middle coils are largest; the end coils smallest.
The coils form a spiral of circles from small to large and back.
Option A shows this.
qs.trap: Expecting evenly spaced circles. The spring's shape sets the circle sizes.

qs.note: They are early electric toasters: bread slices were held against glowing wires by the wire frames, and turned by hand.

steps: From C + D = A + B and A + D < B + C, subtract: A − C < C − A, so A < C.
Then B = C + D − A, and since C > A, B > D.
So the order is Bob > David > Cathy > Alice.
Richest Bob, poorest Alice.

steps: Each pixel of SUGAR must come from exactly one layer: no gaps and no overlaps.
Check one letter at a time: do the two layers fill it together?
Watch for pixels missing or doubled.
Option C combines perfectly.
qs.trap: Checking only one letter. Every letter must be complete.

steps: Each block steps down: a higher bar resting on a lower one.
Arranged in a square, each block's upper part sits over the next one's lower part.
From above you see four L-shapes swirling around a small central square.
Option A shows this.
qs.trap: Drawing a plain grid. The interlocking creates the pinwheel pattern.

steps: A nut cutter is a lever: the hinge is the fulcrum, the nut sits near it and the hand presses at the far end.
Force needed = nut force × (hinge to nut) ÷ (hinge to hand).
The longest handles, with the blade close to the hinge, need the least force.
C has the longest handles.

qs.trap: Choosing by decoration or weight. Only lever lengths matter.

steps: Write the pictured animal's name: FROG, SNAIL, CAT, SPIDER.
The answer starts with the last letter of that name: FROG ends in G, so GOAT.
SNAIL › L › LIZARD. CAT › T › TIGER.
SPIDER ends in R, so RAM.
